desc:
Both arrays a and b are sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain negative numbers, zeros and duplicates. Form all a.length * b.length products a[i] * b[j], sort them in non-decreasing order and return the k-th one (1-indexed). Equal products from different pairs are counted separately.

Example: for a = [-2, 1, 3] and b = [-1, 4] the products are 2, -8, -1, 4, -3, 12, sorted -8, -3, -1, 2, 4, 12, so k = 4 gives 2.
constraints: -40,000 ≤ a[i], b[j] ≤ 40,000 (so every product fits in a 32-bit integer)
hints: Up to 25 million products is too many to sort. Binary search the answer value x and count the products ≤ x.
For one fixed a[i], the condition a[i] * b[j] ≤ x depends on the sign of a[i]: for positive a[i] it holds for a prefix of b, for negative a[i] a suffix, and for zero it holds for all or none.
Positive v: need b[j] ≤ floor(x / v). Negative v: need b[j] ≥ ceil(x / v), which equals -floor(x / (-v)). Use floor division carefully and a bisect on b.
editorial: Let count(x) be the number of pairs with product at most x; it is non-decreasing in x and the answer is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k, searched in [min product, max product] (the extremes are among the four corner products of the sorted arrays).

To compute count(x), handle each v = a[i] by its sign. If v > 0, the valid partners are b[j] ≤ floor(x / v), a prefix found with bisect_right. If v < 0, dividing by a negative flips the inequality: b[j] ≥ ceil(x / v), a suffix found with bisect_left; with integer floor division ceil(x / v) = -floor(x / (-v)). If v = 0, every product is 0, so all |b| pairs count when x ≥ 0 and none otherwise.

The search needs about 32 iterations of an O(|a| log |b|) count, so O(|a| log |b| log R) time and O(1) space. Iterating over the shorter array is faster, since the product is symmetric. The classic mistakes are floor/ceil on negative numbers and treating zero as a positive or negative value.
